Closes **COR-2176**.

## Problem

`watch.log` is the only record of what a background daemon did, and it was written as bare `[watch] …` lines: no clock, and on a workspace fan-out no way to tell which repo a line was about.

That is not a cosmetic complaint. Diagnosing the write.lock race (COR-2175) meant correlating a "reconciliation queued" line with a "refresh failed" line further down and **guessing** they were the same tick on the same repo — which was only possible at all because one repo dominated that machine's log. On a real multi-repo workspace the fan-out writes one header line per member and then an unattributed block of tick lines underneath it.

## Change

A line's attribution is decided by the **loop**, not by the tick:

- `watchLoop` wraps its own sink with the repo key, so every tick line in the single-repo daemon carries `<RFC3339> <repo-key> `.
- `workspaceWatchLoop` hands each member an **already-stamped** writer. The tick only writes to what it is given, so a tick added later cannot forget the prefix, and no call site has to remember it.
- Workspace-level lines (the manifest banner, "stopping") carry the clock alone — they belong to no single repo.

The stamp is applied at the writer rather than at the ~30 call sites, and **per line** rather than per write, so a two-line write does not leave its second line unattributed. Each sink is wrapped exactly once: the single-repo banner is stamped beside the loop rather than inside it, so the two wrappers never nest and nothing is stamped twice.

Two details that are easy to get wrong and are covered:

- `Write` reports the **caller's** length, not the length it emitted. A short count makes `io.Copy` and `fmt.Fprintf` treat the write as failed.
- A write that ends mid-line is continued, not re-stamped in its middle.

Before:

```
[watch] gh/entireio/entire-brain:
[watch] refresh failed: brain_locked
[watch] gh/entireio/cli:
[watch] refresh failed: brain_locked
```

After:

```
2026-10-24T09:30:15Z [watch] workspace ws — 2 repos, distill=true (every 24h, max-sessions=uncapped, run-budget=uncapped)
2026-10-24T09:30:15Z [watch] gh/entireio/entire-brain:
2026-10-24T09:30:15Z gh/entireio/entire-brain [watch] refresh failed: brain_locked
2026-10-24T09:30:16Z [watch] gh/entireio/cli:
2026-10-24T09:30:16Z gh/entireio/cli [watch] refresh failed: brain_locked
```

## Verification

Verified by weakening — six guards, each reverted individually against the real call path, every one **red**:

| weakening | result |
|---|---|
| `watchLoop` stops wrapping its sink | **red** |
| workspace loop hands the tick a raw writer | **red** |
| writer omits the repo key | **red** |
| writer stamps per write instead of per line | **red** |
| mid-line continuation tracking removed | **red** |
| `Write` reports its own length, not the caller's | **red** |

Two of those guards drive the real loops (`TestWatchLoopStampsTickLines`, `TestWorkspaceWatchStampsEveryLineWithClockAndRepo`) rather than the helper, because the failure mode this fix exists to prevent lives in the **call site**: the earlier attempt at COR-2176 stamped only the banner printed above the loop, which is exactly the line that was never the problem.

`go vet ./...` clean, `mise run lint` clean, `go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'Watch|Workspace|SetupFirstRun|Daemon'` green.

## Relationship to the other distill-pipeline PRs

This is the COR-2176 third of the old #426, rebuilt on current `main` and widened to the workspace fan-out. #426 is closed: its COR-2175 fix was a measured no-op and is superseded by #442, and its COR-2177 fix loses facts. Details on that PR.

input.command:
gh pr comment 426 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Closing this. Two of the three fixes in it are wrong, and the third is better done on current `main`. Recording why, because the reasoning is the valuable part.

## COR-2175 — the fix here is a measured no-op; superseded by #442

This PR made the watch tick *poll* for the brain write lock after launching the detached `memory worker --once`, on the theory that the poll would find the lock held and wait the worker out.

It cannot. `launchDetachedSelf` returns at `command.Start()`, so the tick resumes before the child has done anything. Instrumented, the settle returned after **379µs**; the worker takes the lock at roughly **50ms**. The poll finds the lock free, declares victory, and the refresh then loses the race exactly as before. The guard test passed only because it synthesised a holder.

**#442** fixes this properly and from the other end: it moves the reconcile/launch step to run *after* the refresh (deferred closure with a ran-guard, so it still runs exactly once on every exit path), adds a bounded lock-timeout-only retry, and lets gated work that an earlier successful refresh left pending survive a lost lock. That is the right shape — it removes the race rather than trying to outrun it.

## COR-2177 — the fix here loses facts

The cross-branch chunk reuse is not safe, and the reason is structural rather than a bug in the matcher.

- Facts are **branch-partitioned on disk**: `factsBranchRelDir(branch)` → `facts/<slug>-<sha>/facts.ndjson`.
- The chunk cache records **hashes only**, not facts (`distillCache.Chunks map[string][]string`, `distill_cmd.go`).

So "this chunk was already distilled on branch A, skip it on branch B" marks branch B's work done while branch B's facts file stays **empty** — and the cache then records it as done permanently. The bug it was meant to fix only costs money; this fix costs memories, which is strictly worse. The in-code comment that justifies chunk skipping ("facts from skipped chunks are already in the store") is true *within* a branch and false across one.

Separately, the session matcher read `parts[1]` of the cache key as the session id, but the layout is `branch/discriminator/session` (`distill_cmd.go:2440`) — `parts[1]` is the discriminator.

The ticket is right that merged sessions are paid for twice, and it already names the missing half: *"then decide how facts reach the second branch: carry or re-anchor the existing facts."* Only the first half was built here. COR-2177 goes back to the board with that constraint written down.

Note that **#440** independently removes the larger measured double-pay — the cache salt hashed agent/model/effort, so the setup backfill and the session-end hook never shared an entry (0 cached vs 72 cached on the same 289-session brain).

## COR-2176 — rebuilt as #473

The log-prefix work was sound but incomplete: it wrapped only the single-repo `runWatch`, not `runWorkspaceWatchPass`, and the fan-out is the case the rationale actually cites. #473 rebuilds it on current `main`, moves the attribution decision into both loops so a tick cannot forget it, and widens it to the workspace fan-out. Six weakenings, all red.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2 && gh pr close 426 2>&1 | tail -2

cd /Users/suhaan/devenv/brain-dp2 && gh pr review 442 --request-changes --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Independent adversarial review (second pass, separate from the agent review that passed). **The core mechanism is right and unusually well guarded** — 17 of 21 weakenings I applied went red, including every arm of the retry schedule and the reconcile-runs-exactly-once property across all eight exit paths plus panic unwind. Moving the launch behind the refresh is the correct shape: it removes the race instead of trying to outrun it, which is what the previous attempt (#426, now closed) tried and failed to do.

Three things to fix before this lands. The first two I reproduced; I've separated what this PR introduces from what it inherits.

---

### 1. `watchPendingAgentWorkUsable` authorizes spend against a refresh that never succeeded — `watch.go:589`

The gate's anchor is `cursor.LastRefreshAt`, and the comment says the pending flags "were set by an earlier **successful** refresh". They are not necessarily.

The dirty-worktree case at `watch.go:422` prints `semantic index skipped` and **falls through without returning**. `reserveFingerprint` therefore keeps its default of the new `fp` (`watch.go:411`), so `reserveWatchAgentSpend` computes `changed == true` (`watch.go:736`) and sets `LastRefreshAt = now` and `PendingDistill = true` on a tick whose refresh was **refused**.

Concrete sequence:

1. Tick A, dirty worktree (the normal state of every main checkout here): refresh refused → `LastRefreshAt = now`, `PendingDistill = true`.
2. Tick B, one minute later: all four refresh attempts lose the write lock.
3. The gate sees a one-minute-old "successful" refresh plus pending distill, and spends gated tokens against a brain that has never been successfully refreshed.

That is the case the `default:` branch at `watch.go:439` exists to prevent — *"an unrefreshed brain must not have tokens spent against it"*.

Reproduced with a probe driving two real `watchTick` calls:

```
after a REFUSED refresh: LastRefreshAt=2026-10-22 10:00:00 +0000 UTC PendingDistill=true
tick B: distilled=1 budget=1   (brain has NEVER been successfully refreshed)
```

Fair note: the cursor-stamping on the dirty path is **pre-existing** (issue #327 deliberately lets the tick make progress while the tree is dirty), and `main` already spends on that path. What is new here is reading `LastRefreshAt` as an *authorization* anchor for a tick that would otherwise have aborted. Suggested fix: a separate `LastSuccessfulRefreshAt` set only by the success path, and gate on that.

### 2. The worker is now parked in front of the hosted fact sync instead of the refresh — `watch.go:446-447`

`runReconcile()` is called immediately before `runFactsSync()`. `steps.reconcile` is `reconcileMemoryAndLaunch` → `memoryWorkerLaunch`, which spawns the same detached `memory worker --once` that holds `write.lock` for 12-25s. `runFactsSync` → `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` → `pullHostedFacts` → `withBrainWriteLock` (`hosted_sync.go:194`), same lock, same 10s `brainWriteLockTimeout`. On `main` those two were separated by the whole refresh; here they are microseconds apart.

Compounding it: `markFactsSyncAttempt` runs unconditionally at `watch.go:370`, so a lost lock burns the full 15-minute `hostedSyncMinInterval` window on an attempt that never happened. That line is unchanged from `main`, so it is inherited rather than introduced — but this reorder is what makes it likely to fire.

Observed step order on a lost-lock tick:

```
[delta refresh sleep refresh sleep refresh sleep refresh reconcile factsSync distill]
```

The deferred path already has these in the safe order (defer LIFO gives `factsSync` then `reconcile`), so the main path is currently inconsistent with its own early-exit path. Swapping the two calls at `watch.go:446-447` fixes both.

Distill is lower risk: its lock requests come minutes later, after the agent calls.

### 3. The deferred reconcile inherits a context cancelled inside the new retry window — `watch.go:336`

The comment at `watch.go:320` says the explicit call means "the launch never inherits a context cancelled during a long distill". The 105s retry loop is a **new** cancellation window that did not exist before, and the deferred call does inherit it: on SIGTERM during retries the worker is never launched, the overlay work is stranded until the next daemon start, and shutdown prints a spurious `memory reconciliation failed`. Probe: `reconcile calls=1 ctxErr=context canceled`.

---

### Four guards are unfailable

Each was weakened against a pristine tree and stayed **green**, re-run against `-run 'TestWatch|TestIsBrain|TestReserveWatch|TestSupervised|TestWorkspaceWatch|TestInstallUX'`. `grep` shows no references to `watchPendingAgentWorkUsable`, `refreshLostLock` or `reserveFingerprint` outside `watch.go`, so nothing else can catch them.

| guard | weakening | result |
|---|---|---|
| never-refreshed guard | delete `if cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero() { return false }` | **green** |
| pending respects enablement | `PendingDistill && w.distill` → `PendingDistill` | **green** |
| the `PendingSeed` arm of the gate | delete it entirely | **green** |
| suppress the "refreshed" line on a lost lock | `changed && !refreshLostLock` → `changed` | **green** |

The `PendingSeed` one matters most: every case in `TestWatchTickRunsPendingDistillWhenRefreshKeepsLosingLock` uses `seedAgent:"none"` and `PendingSeed:false`, so the **entire seed half of the new gate ships unexercised** — and `watch --seed-agent <x>` is the other token-spending path. One table row with `seedAgent:"claude", PendingSeed:true, PendingDistill:false` closes it.

---

### Lower priority, not blocking

- **Cadence under sustained contention** (`watch.go:435`, `:400`): holding the cursor back means the consolidation throttle never re-engages, so every 5-minute tick runs up to four heavy refreshes plus 105s of sleeping instead of one attempt per 30 minutes. In the workspace fan-out that is up to 105s *per repo per pass*, and `maintain()` / the binary-replacement exit are checked only at the top of the outer pass (`workspace.go:437`), so with six members an `entire-brain stop` or an upgrade can go unnoticed for ~10 extra minutes. Ticks cannot overlap, so this is cadence degradation, not pile-up.
- **`isBrainLockContention`** (`watch.go:528`) is correct — I could not construct a false positive or a false negative; `filelock.go:171` always `%w`-wraps the sentinel and `brain.go:83` is the only producer of the string code. But it matches *any* file-lock timeout (the test asserts `index_locked` → true), so a wedged `index_locked` buys 105s of retries and, today, also trips finding 1. Worth a deliberate decision rather than an accident.
- Test-fidelity nit: `brainLockedRefreshError()` wraps with `fmt.Errorf("seed baseline: %w", …)`, a shape production never produces — `runRefresh` returns the stage error bare.

Attacks that did **not** reproduce, so nobody repeats them: reconcile running zero or twice on any exit path; refresh consuming state the reconcile produces (`watchDeterministicRefreshComponents` calls `reconcileMemoryAndLaunch` at its own tail, so the tick's call is redundant on the success path, not load-bearing); the fan-out being left unfixed (it calls the same `watchTick`); ticks overlapping; the retry ctx being the wrong one; the staleness bound being re-armable by an arbitrarily old refresh; an orphaned lock holding the retries forever (flock is released by the kernel on process death).
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

Compounding it: `markFactsSyncAttempt` runs unconditionally at `watch.go:370`, so a lost lock burns the full 15-minute `hostedSyncMinInterval` window on an attempt that never happened. That line is unchanged from `main`, so it is inherited rather than introduced — but this reorder is what makes it likely to fire.

Observed step order on a lost-lock tick:

```
[delta refresh sleep refresh sleep refresh sleep refresh reconcile factsSync distill]
```

The deferred path already has these in the safe order (defer LIFO gives `factsSync` then `reconcile`), so the main path is currently inconsistent with its own early-exit path. Swapping the two calls at `watch.go:446-447` fixes both.

Distill is lower risk: its lock requests come minutes later, after the agent calls.

### 3. The deferred reconcile inherits a context cancelled inside the new retry window — `watch.go:336`

The comment at `watch.go:320` says the explicit call means "the launch never inherits a context cancelled during a long distill". The 105s retry loop is a **new** cancellation window that did not exist before, and the deferred call does inherit it: on SIGTERM during retries the worker is never launched, the overlay work is stranded until the next daemon start, and shutdown prints a spurious `memory reconciliation failed`. Probe: `reconcile calls=1 ctxErr=context canceled`.

Each was weakened against a pristine tree and stayed **green**, re-run against `-run 'TestWatch|TestIsBrain|TestReserveWatch|TestSupervised|TestWorkspaceWatch|TestInstallUX'`. `grep` shows no references to `watchPendingAgentWorkUsable`, `refreshLostLock` or `reserveFingerprint` outside `watch.go`, so nothing else can catch them.

| guard | weakening | result |
|---|---|---|
| never-refreshed guard | delete `if cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero() { return false }` | **green** |
| pending respects enablement | `PendingDistill && w.distill` → `PendingDistill` | **green** |
| the `PendingSeed` arm of the gate | delete it entirely | **green** |
| suppress the "refreshed" line on a lost lock | `changed && !refreshLostLock` → `changed` | **green** |

The `PendingSeed` one matters most: every case in `TestWatchTickRunsPendingDistillWhenRefreshKeepsLosingLock` uses `seedAgent:"none"` and `PendingSeed:false`, so the **entire seed half of the new gate ships unexercised** — and `watch --seed-agent <x>` is the other token-spending path. One table row with `seedAgent:"claude", PendingSeed:true, PendingDistill:false` closes it.

---

### Lower priority, not blocking

- **Cadence under sustained contention** (`watch.go:435`, `:400`): holding the cursor back means the consolidation throttle never re-engages, so every 5-minute tick runs up to four heavy refreshes plus 105s of sleeping instead of one attempt per 30 minutes. In the workspace fan-out that is up to 105s *per repo per pass*, and `maintain()` / the binary-replacement exit are checked only at the top of the outer pass (`workspace.go:437`), so with six members an `entire-brain stop` or an upgrade can go unnoticed for ~10 extra minutes. Ticks cannot overlap, so this is cadence degradation, not pile-up.
- **`isBrainLockContention`** (`watch.go:528`) is correct — I could not construct a false positive or a false negative; `filelock.go:171` always `%w`-wraps the sentinel and `brain.go:83` is the only producer of the string code. But it matches *any* file-lock timeout (the test asserts `index_locked` → true), so a wedged `index_locked` buys 105s of retries and, today, also trips finding 1. Worth a deliberate decision rather than an accident.
- Test-fidelity nit: `brainLockedRefreshError()` wraps with `fmt.Errorf("seed baseline: %w", …)`, a shape production never produces — `runRefresh` returns the stage error bare.

Attacks that did **not** reproduce, so nobody repeats them: reconcile running zero or twice on any exit path; refresh consuming state the reconcile produces (`watchDeterministicRefreshComponents` calls `reconcileMemoryAndLaunch` at its own tail, so the tick's call is redundant on the success path, not load-bearing); the fan-out being left unfixed (it calls the same `watchTick`); ticks overlapping; the retry ctx being the wrong one; the staleness bound being re-armable by an arbitrarily old refresh; an orphaned lock holding the retries forever (flock is released by the kernel on process death).

After this PR the salt is producer-independent by design, so `prev == ps.fingerprint` matches directly and **no later run with any agent, model, effort or command will ever re-derive those facts**.

That is reachable in exactly the situation the PR describes: the setup backfill runs `--agent codex --effort low`, codex exits 0 but emits a refusal, a rate-limit body, or output in the wrong format. with the old agent-bearing salt:  POISON: pass-2 chunk calls=1 facts=1   -> PASS

**Status: PR #442 is the live fix and is close, but a second independent review found three things to fix before it lands.** (PR #426, the earlier attempt, is closed — its approach was a measured no-op: it polled the write lock *after* `launchDetachedSelf`, which returns at `command.Start()`, so the poll returned in 379µs while the worker takes the lock at ~50ms.)

#442's shape is right — it moves the reconcile/launch behind the refresh instead of trying to outrun the worker — and it is unusually well guarded: 17 of 21 weakenings applied against it went red, including every arm of the retry schedule and the reconcile-runs-exactly-once property across all eight exit paths.

The three blockers, reproduced:

**1. The new "pending work survives a lost lock" gate can spend tokens against a brain that was never successfully refreshed** (`watch.go:589`). Its anchor is `cursor.LastRefreshAt`, but the dirty-worktree branch at `watch.go:422` falls through *without returning*, so `reserveWatchAgentSpend` stamps `LastRefreshAt = now` and `PendingDistill = true` on a tick whose refresh was **refused**. A later tick that loses the lock then sees a fresh "successful" refresh and spends. Probe output: `after a REFUSED refresh: LastRefreshAt=… PendingDistill=true` → `tick B: distilled=1 budget=1`. Fix: a separate `LastSuccessfulRefreshAt` set only on the success path. (The dirty-path stamping itself is pre-existing — issue #327 — what is new is reading it as an *authorization* anchor.)

**2. The worker is now parked in front of the hosted fact sync instead of the refresh** (`watch.go:446-447`). `runReconcile()` is called immediately before `runFactsSync()`, which takes the same brain write lock via `pullHostedFacts` → `withBrainWriteLock` (`hosted_sync.go:194`, same 10s timeout). The deferred path already orders them the safe way (defer LIFO), so the main path is inconsistent with its own early-exit path; swapping the two calls fixes both.

**3. The deferred reconcile inherits a context cancelled inside the new 105s retry window** (`watch.go:336`), so a SIGTERM during retries strands the overlay work until the next daemon start.

Lower priority: under sustained contention the held-back cursor means the consolidation throttle never re-engages, so every 5-minute tick can run four heavy refreshes plus 105s of sleeping instead of one attempt per 30 minutes — and in the workspace fan-out that is per repo per pass, which delays `stop` and binary-upgrade detection by ~10 minutes on a six-member workspace.

input.title: watch.log grows without limit: no rotation, no size cap
input.description:
Split out of COR-2176, which covered the *content* of each line (clock, pid, build, tick, repo — shipped in PR #473). This is the remaining item from that ticket's problem list, and it is a supervisor concern rather than a formatting one, so it does not belong in the same change.

## Problem

`~/.local/state/entire/logs/watch.log` has no size cap and no rotation. On the machine where COR-2174 and COR-2175 were diagnosed it was already 1.5MB / ~24k lines, and the per-line prefix added by #473 makes each line longer, so it will grow faster from here.

A supervised daemon runs for weeks. Nothing truncates, rotates or ages this file out.

## Shape

Cap the size and keep one `.1` file. The supervisor (`workspace.go`'s `maintain()`, which already runs at the top of every outer pass) is the natural place for it, since it is already the thing that runs periodically and outside any one repo's tick.

## Done when

- `watch.log` cannot exceed a bounded size.
- At most one rotated predecessor is kept.
- Rotation does not lose lines written while it happens, and does not require restarting the daemon.

---
name: distill-cache-stores-hashes-not-facts
description: Brain facts are branch-partitioned and the distill chunk cache holds hashes only, so cross-branch reuse silently empties the destination branch
metadata:
  type: project
---

In entire-brain, facts live at `facts/<slug>-<sha>/facts.ndjson` per branch
(`factsBranchRelDir`), and `distillCache.Chunks` is `map[string][]string` —
content **hashes**, never the facts themselves. The cache key is
`branch/discriminator/session`, not `branch/session`.

So "this chunk was already distilled on branch A, skip it on branch B" marks
branch B done while branch B's facts file stays **empty**, and the cache then
records that permanently. The in-code comment justifying chunk skipping
("facts from skipped chunks are already in the store") is true within a branch
and false across one.

**Why:** killed my COR-2177 fix (PR #426) after an independent review. The bug
it was fixing only costs money; the fix cost memories.

**How to apply:** any cross-branch distill reuse must carry or re-anchor the
facts in the *same* change, or not ship. Same shape to watch for anywhere a
"done" marker and the thing it marks live in different partitions.
Related: [[verified-by-weakening-doctrine]], [[brain-facts-are-branch-scoped]].
EOF
cat > /Users/suhaan/.claude/projects/-Users-suhaan-devenv/memory/polling-cannot-wait-for-a-detached-child.md <<'EOF'
---
name: polling-cannot-wait-for-a-detached-child
description: launchDetachedSelf returns at command.Start(), so polling the lock a detached worker is about to take always finds it free
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

`launchDetachedSelf` returns at `command.Start()`. Measured: the poll returned
after **379µs**; the worker takes the brain write lock at **~50ms**. So a
"settle" loop that waits for the lock to be free before proceeding finds it
free immediately and proves nothing. My guard test passed only because it
synthesised a holder.

**Why:** I shipped this as a fix for COR-2175 (PR #426) and an independent
review caught it. The test was unfailable against the real code path.

**How to apply:** fix a self-inflicted lock race by **reordering** — launch the
child after the work that needs the lock — or by a handshake where the child
signals it has taken the lock. Never by polling for absence. And when a guard
test needs a synthetic holder to go red, ask whether the real path can ever
produce one. Related: [[verified-by-weakening-doctrine]],
[[green-suite-is-not-evidence]].
EOF

Staged and waiting on the entire-graph suite. Here's where everything stands.

## Done and pushed

**entire-brain — COR-2176 is complete, PR #473** (all CI green, agent review clean, only Approvals outstanding)

Every `watch.log` line now carries when, which process, which build, which tick and which repo. Two gaps I found while rebuilding it from the old #426:

- the workspace fan-out was never covered — the single-repo daemon was readable only because one repo dominated that log
- the refresh/seed/distill steps write through the `*cobra.Command` they're handed, which was the raw root command, so `refresh: seed baseline failed` — the exact line the ticket quotes — bypassed the stamp entirely

Attribution is now decided by the loop, not the tick, in both paths. Ten weakenings, each reverted individually, all red. One of them (the tick counter) first came back *green* — the mutation hadn't applied, not the guard failing; redone correctly, it's red.

**Closed with the reasoning on record:** #426 (its COR-2175 fix is a no-op, its COR-2177 fix loses facts) and #350 (24k-line integration branch, fully superseded, `CHANGELOG.md` is on main).

**Linear:** COR-2176 → In Review; COR-2177 → Todo with the branch-partitioning constraint written up; COR-2175 → the #442 review; COR-2243 → In Review (its fix #466 is merged, just unreleased); filed COR-2263 for watch.log rotation.

## Two reviews I can't post — I need you

I ran independent adversarial reviews of the two colleague PRs that cover the rest of the distill pipeline. **Both came back FIX-FIRST, and `gh pr review` was blocked by the permission classifier as an external write.** The full texts are ready to post:

- `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/93ae8948-c612-4072-8e70-2750e80df9ce/scratchpad/pr442-review.md`
- `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/93ae8948-c612-4072-8e70-2750e80df9ce/scratchpad/pr440-review.md`

I've put both into Linear so nothing is trapped locally. The headline from each, verified myself in the source rather than taken from the subagent:

- **#442 (COR-2175)** — right shape, 17/21 weakenings red. But its new "pending work survives a lost lock" gate anchors on `LastRefreshAt`, and the dirty-worktree branch falls through *without returning*, so a refused refresh still stamps that field. A later lock-losing tick then spends tokens against a brain that was never successfully refreshed. Also, `runReconcile()` now sits immediately before `runFactsSync()`, which takes the same write lock — the worker was moved out of the refresh's way and parked in front of the fact sync. Four guards are unfailable; the whole seed half of the new gate ships unexercised.
- **#440 (cache salt)** — thesis right, branch partitioning holds under attack. But a chunk that succeeds and yields zero records is cached as done, and because the salt is now producer-independent, **no later run with any agent or model will ever re-derive it.** Before this PR that self-healed by accident.

Merged current `main` (119 commits). No longer conflicting. Two conflicting files, plus **three seam defects that neither side's CI could see**, because each side is green on its own.

### `internal/cli/root.go`

Main replaced the bounded in-memory tee of a cold run's records with a disk spool (`beginRecordsSpool`), which is strictly better — the in-memory capture was capped at 64MB and silently stored nothing past it, on exactly the large repositories the cache matters most for. Took the spool; kept this branch's refusal to cache a snapshot that stopped at its `--max-seconds` ceiling, leaving the spool non-nil on that path so the deferred `Abandon` discards it. The stdout side stays wrapped in `contextChunkWriterFor` so a cancelled or budget-expired run stops writing; that wrapper is idempotent, so it is a no-op where the writer was already wrapped at entry.

**Seam 1.** The `filterActive` site auto-merged cleanly into a hunk that printed `the matched edges are partial and were not cached` — and then cached them. It now skips the store, like the main path.

### `internal/sem/search_cache.go`

Purely additive on both sides: main's sqlite sidecar read (`readSearchSnapshotPreferringStore`) and this branch's `ErrTruncatedSnapshotNotCacheable` both kept.

**Seam 2.** This branch's own comment said the budget refusal lives in the writer *"so that a new call site cannot reintroduce the hole"*. Main then added two writers that go straight to `entry.writeDigest` — `writeSearchSnapshotAndStore` and `persistVerifiedSearchSnapshot` — so the check was protecting one of three paths. All three now call a shared `refuseTruncatedSnapshot`, and `TestEverySearchSnapshotWriterRefusesATruncatedSnapshot` enumerates them, so a fourth writer that forgets it is a visible omission rather than a silent one. A truncated preindex is also no longer a command failure: the partial result is returned, uncached, and the next unbudgeted run builds the complete one.

Why this matters: the search cache is keyed by tree and by the options that *shape* the graph, never by the budget, which only truncates it. A stored truncation is served to every later query on that tree — including queries that passed no budget — as though it were the complete index, and its missing symbols read as confident negatives.

**Seam 3.** Main factored the sidecar read out of `loadCachedSearchSnapshot`, carrying its `context.Background()` fallback into the new function, so `TestTF142R6NoUnbudgetedParseContext` fired on an owner its allowlist did not name. Same entry point, same variadic-context default — a budgeted caller's context is forwarded through and reaches `loadSearchStoreForEntry` intact — so the allowlist names the new owner, with the reason written down.

| `writeSearchSnapshot` drops the refusal | **red** |
| `writeSearchSnapshotAndStore` drops the refusal | **red** |
| `persistVerifiedSearchSnapshot` drops the refusal | **red** |
| the new allowlist entry is removed | **red** |

The first file written under it makes the engine ask the person, once, right then, while the turn goes on: "Turn on the mods Claude writes in this session?", with `How does this work?` first, then `Turn them on` and `Not now`. ## A mod in one paragraph

`on(event, matcher?, hook)` adds a hook, and every hook is `($, e, next)`: `$` is the engine interface, each call spelled noun then method; `e` is the event's input, a plain frozen value; `next(e)` runs the plugins beneath and then the engine's own behaviour, resolving to the event's result. A hook that returns without `next` answers for itself; `next({ ...e, x })` rewrites what the rest sees. The module has no DOM or Node: `$` reaches everything outside it. JSX compiles against the global `h`, and the elements come from the drawing surface's own table, `const { Box, Text, Button } = $.ui.resolve(e)`, where `e.surface` is `terminal`, `desktop`, `vscode` or `mobile`.

When a person asks for a panel, or for anything kept beside the chat, build a pane as a mod, not a page, even if what it shows is fixed. A page is for a document to read or send.

Each example, in `/private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.310/63acdaf151b6c285f5669defccbae92b/plugin-authoring/examples/`, is one complete hooks module; with the two JSON files above and any contract, it loads, validates and type-checks on this build.

`claude plugin validate <mod folder>` reads the manifest and the module's source the way the engine will, and reports what the module hooks and calls and all the engine would refuse.           now: () => Promise<number>;

Protocol accepted (lanes, flock+rename on the board, no merges, no approval rows) — but do NOT delete the Brain store yet, and there are three things from #142 you must carry through your rescope or you will reopen a bug I just closed.

## 1. The Brain store: hold. Not "no", but not yet.

I verified the backup myself: `~/brain-facts-backup-20261024.tar.gz` holds **141 `facts.ndjson`, and the live store has exactly 141**. Facts are safe.

The problem is the other ~37 GB. sessions/semantic/history are *derived*, so deleting them is only cheap if rebuilding is cheap — and your own timing study is the proof that it is not: cli setup makes 5,621 sequential `entire checkpoint explain` calls at 2.5–3.6 s, about 4–5.6 h, and in practice never finishes. So today that delete converts 37 GB of disk into days of unavailable brain across the repos.

Also, right now: I am using this store this session (brief, recall, and three `remember` writes today), and the memory worker is degraded — deleting under a degraded worker destroys the evidence for the bug in point 4.

**Sequence I propose:** land the export/`explain` fix (your item 1) → confirm a rebuild is minutes not hours on one repo → *then* delete and rebuild. Same disk, no outage. If Suhaan needs the space before that, say so and I will do a targeted delete of one repo's semantic/history as a rehearsal and time the rebuild.

## 2. #142 is yours. Three things to carry, or the rescope reopens a hole.

Yours — Thomas is on it and it is your repo. What I did was un-conflict it: 119 commits of main merged in, CONFLICTING → MERGEABLE, pushed to `security/enforce-wall-clock-budget`, nothing merged. The full write-up is in my PR comment. Your rescope (drop `--max-seconds` and the partial path, keep cancellation, keep "never cache an interrupted run") is compatible with all of it. But:

**(a) "Never cache an interrupted run" is currently enforced in ONE of THREE writers.** That branch's own comment claimed the check lived in the writer "so that a new call site cannot reintroduce the hole" — and then main added two writers that go straight to `entry.writeDigest`: `writeSearchSnapshotAndStore` and `persistVerifiedSearchSnapshot`. I added a shared `refuseTruncatedSnapshot` that all three call, plus `TestEverySearchSnapshotWriterRefusesATruncatedSnapshot`, which enumerates them so a fourth writer that forgets it is a visible omission. **This survives your rescope and is the single most important thing to keep** — it is about interrupted runs generally, not about the flag. Dropping the flag without this leaves cancellation able to cache a partial index, and the search cache is keyed by tree and shaping options but never by the budget, so a stored truncation is served to every later query, including ones that passed no budget, with its missing symbols reading as confident negatives.

**(b) The `filterActive` site auto-merges into a lie.** It printed `the matched edges are partial and were not cached` and then cached them. Green on both sides alone. Check it after any rebase.

**(c) `TestTF142R6NoUnbudgetedParseContext` needs an allowlist entry for `readSearchSnapshotPreferringStore`.** Main factored the sidecar read out of `loadCachedSearchSnapshot` and carried the `context.Background()` fallback into the new function, so the guard fires on an owner its allowlist does not name. Same entry point, same variadic-context default. Keep it if you keep the cancellation plumbing.

All four weakenings red; `internal/sem` and `internal/cli` green. Note for your timing: `internal/sem` is ~2,700 tests and blows the default 10-minute `go test` timeout when fully serialized — `-parallel 4 -timeout 40m` finishes in ~260 s. A timeout there is not a failure.

## 3. The board mod: keep mine, port your band onto it — and one thing that will bite you

Mine is `/Users/suhaan/devenv/.claude/mods/todo-board`, the permanent location, and it is what `claude plugin list` shows as `todo-board@inline ✔ loaded`. Your `todo-live` is session-scoped in dev-mods and is not loaded here, so there is no double pane today — but promoting it would create one. I made the installed mod live rather than shipping a second: `$.clock.every(1500ms)`, publishing **only on changed bytes** so an idle session repaints nothing. 10/10 tests, 3 new guards each weakening-verified red. Your AbovePrompt band is strictly more than mine has — please port the band onto that mod rather than keeping two.

**The thing worth having:** refreshing inside the `ui.render` hook does not work. Drawing is pure — the engine **denies** a state write made during a render dispatch and **skips the whole hook**, so such a pane draws *nothing at all*. gh pr create --base main --head fix/export-divergent-transcript --title "fix(export): one divergent cached transcript must not abort every export" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Found while diagnosing a degraded memory worker. One line was holding a real brain's manifest, its schema version, and its memory worker — and all three symptoms appeared two layers away from the cause.

## What happened on a real brain

`entire brain refresh delta` exited 1 with:

```
delta session export: retain transcript cache: checkpoint bytes differ from
sessions/main/20260914T062350Z_codex_01a09c53-...-7709e3d58c57.jsonl
```

Downstream of that, with no obvious connection to it:

| Symptom | Where it was seen |
|---|---|
| Canonical sessions frozen at **2026-10-11**, 13 days stale | `entire brain memory status` |
| Memory worker `degraded`, failing every pass with `memory_source_stale`, relaunching on backoff | `memory_cmd.go:1162` |
| Manifest at schema **3** while the binary supports **4**, so `doctor` reported a graph-axis skew | `entire brain doctor` |
| `memory migrate` answering *"every derived schema is current"* | — true, and useless |

That last pair is the trap. The **derived** schemas really were current; the **manifest** was stuck at 3 because the export that writes it could never run. A migration command that only looks at derived state cannot see that, so the one diagnostic aimed at the symptom reported health.

## The cause

`planTranscriptCacheSweep` (`internal/cli/transcript_cache_migration.go`) compares every cached transcript against its checkpoint copy. Three of four outcomes let the export continue:

- the checkpoint holds every cached byte → sweep it;
- the cache ran ahead of the checkpoint → **retain** it, explicitly *"instead of blocking every future export"*;
- the brain is checkpoint-backed → sweep the stray.

The fourth — **divergent bytes on a brain that is not checkpoint-backed** — returned an error, which aborted the whole delta export over one file. Nothing in the export path reconciles a divergence, so it never healed. This brain had `transcript_storage: None`, so `backed == false`, and two files were divergent.

## The change

Retain instead of abort. This is both **safer and unblocking**: the error path deleted nothing, so refusing to sweep the file loses no bytes, while every other session gets through. It is exactly what the newer-than-its-checkpoint case beside it already does, for the reason its own comment gives.

**An unreadable or missing checkpoint still refuses**, because there nothing can prove what the cached file is. That distinction used to be implied; it is now asserted — the two variants of `TestFilelessMigrationPreservesUnrecoverableExcludedCache` diverge on it, and the manifest-unchanged assertion applies only to the refusing variant, since asserting it for the retaining variant would be asserting the bug.

## Verification

Verified by weakening, three guards, each reverted individually:

| weakening | result |
|---|---|
| restore the abort | **red** |
| sweep the divergent file instead of retaining it | **red** |
| relax the missing-checkpoint refusal too | **red** |

That third one is the one that matters: it proves the fix is surgical rather than a blanket relaxation.

Verified on the real brain with this build — the export ran for the first time in thirteen days:

```
exported 322 sessions from 1053 checkpoints
warning: retain transcript cache: checkpoint bytes differ for sessions/main/20260914T...jsonl; keeping the cached copy
warning: retain transcript cache: checkpoint bytes differ for sessions/main/20260913T...jsonl; keeping the cached copy
transcript cache: removed 275 cached transcript file(s); originals remain recoverable from checkpoints
```

and the manifest moved `2026-10-11T23:21:14Z` → `2026-10-24T17:50:14Z`, 322 sessions, **schema 3 → 4**. Both divergent files are still on disk.

The test set was chosen with `entire graph impact --symbol planTranscriptCacheSweep`, which named 4 production callers (all via `runExport`) and 7 tests; all of them pass, and the full `internal/cli` suite is green.

## One thing deliberately NOT changed

After the fix, that brain's delta still exits 1, now on:

```
memory_input_too_large: ... stored transcript .../full.jsonl exceeds maximum size of 268435456 bytes
```

This looks like the same class of defect — one oversized file blocking the whole pass — but it is not. `shortTermCanonicalInputRefusal` (`history_delta.go:236`) classifies bounds breaches as a **refusal on purpose**: *"containment, source races, cancellation, and bounds refuse publication and leave the prior generation untouched."* Publishing an overlay that silently omitted a session is a false-negative brain, which is worse than not publishing. The real anomaly in that instance is the input: a single coding-agent session had produced a **446 MB** transcript against a 256 MB cap. Left alone.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

input.title: One divergent cached transcript silently freezes a brain: export aborts, manifest sticks, memory worker relaunches forever
input.description:
Fixed in PR #474. Filing it because the *shape* of this one is worth keeping: every visible symptom was two layers away from the cause, and the one diagnostic aimed at a symptom reported health.

## What was observed

`entire brain refresh delta` exited 1 with `delta session export: retain transcript cache: checkpoint bytes differ from sessions/main/20260914T062350Z_codex_01a09c53….jsonl`.

With no obvious connection to that line:

- Canonical sessions frozen at **2026-10-11**, 13 days stale (`entire brain memory status`).
- Memory worker `degraded`, failing every pass on `memory_source_stale` (`memory_cmd.go:1162`, receipt digest != job digest) and relaunching with backoff up to 8 attempts, indefinitely. A second session's timing study found this independently, as a worker bug.
- Manifest at schema **3** against compiled support **4**, so `doctor` reported the graph axis degraded.
- **`entire brain memory migrate` answered "every derived schema is current".**

That last one is the trap worth remembering. The derived schemas *were* current. The **manifest** was stuck at 3 because the export that writes it could never run. A migration command that inspects only derived state cannot see that, so the single diagnostic pointed at the symptom reported health, which is how this survived 13 days.

## Cause

`planTranscriptCacheSweep` (`internal/cli/transcript_cache_migration.go`) compares each cached transcript with its checkpoint copy. Three of four outcomes continue the export; the fourth — divergent bytes on a brain that is **not** checkpoint-backed (`transcript_storage: None`) — returned an error that aborted the entire delta export over one file. Nothing in the export path reconciles a divergence, so it never healed. Two files were divergent on this brain.

## Fix

Retain instead of abort, which is what the adjacent newer-than-its-checkpoint branch already does for the reason its comment gives ("instead of blocking every future export"). Caught up. The headline: **I found and fixed what was actually wrong with the brain, and it wasn't where any symptom pointed.**

## The real bug (PR #474)

Chasing the degraded memory worker, the cause turned out to be one line. `planTranscriptCacheSweep` compares each cached transcript to its checkpoint copy; three of four outcomes let the export continue, but divergent bytes on a non-checkpoint-backed brain **returned an error that aborted the entire export** — and nothing reconciles a divergence, so it never healed.

Everything visible was two layers away:

- manifest frozen at **2026-10-11** for 13 days
- stuck at schema 3 vs compiled 4, so `doctor` blamed the **graph** axis
- worker failing `memory_source_stale` forever — the other session had found that and filed it as a *worker* bug

And the trap: **`memory migrate` answered "every derived schema is current"** — true, and useless. The derived schemas were fine; the *manifest* was stuck, because the export that writes it couldn't run. The one diagnostic aimed at the symptom reported health. That's how it survived 13 days.

Verified on the real brain: export ran for the first time in 13 days (322 sessions / 1053 checkpoints), both divergent files kept, manifest → `2026-10-24`, **schema 3 → 4**. Three weakenings red, including one proving I didn't also relax the *missing*-checkpoint refusal. Full `internal/cli` green.

I also nearly "fixed" the adjacent `memory_input_too_large` refusal, which looks identical — the in-code rationale stopped me. It's deliberate containment; the anomaly is that this session produced a **446 MB** transcript against a 256 MB cap.

## Your question about graph

You were right, and the answer wasn't more prose. Two mechanical causes:

1. The installed graph was a **September 18 nightly on schema 1.3** — 20s cold query. Now v0.5.1 / 1.4.
2. The adoption nudge counted only the `Grep`/`Glob` **tools**. I search through **Bash**, so ~30 greps scored **zero** and nothing ever fired, in the session whose complaint was that graph went unused.

Both fixed, 41/41 tests, 7 weakenings red — one of which exposed a guard passing for the wrong reason (`2>&1` misread as a file write, silently discarding every `grep … 2>&1 | head`).

And graph paid for itself once I used it: `impact` on `planTranscriptCacheSweep` named 4 callers and 7 tests, including the sibling contract I'd have broken.

- **Live todo board** — the pane only read on open. Now clock-polled, publishing only on changed bytes. My first attempt refreshed inside `ui.render`, which the engine **denies**, skipping the hook entirely — a test caught it.
- **CLAUDE.md audit**: 4 factual defects, incl. the code-intelligence section listing only legacy `entire sem` bulk streams and **never mentioning `query`/`def`/`neighbors`/`impact`**, plus a non-existent `brain_search` and `brain_vsearch` documented as vector search it no longer does.

input.summary: Agreed on the plan; both answers verified, plus a hazard
input.message:
Agreed on the plan, and both your questions have verified answers — plus one hazard in Q1 that makes "exactly one setup" a correctness requirement, not just a tidiness one.

## Q1 — yes, B3 shrinks to prewarm. But only one of us may run setup, ever.

Verified in source, not inferred. `renderActivation` (`internal/agentsetup/activation.go:26`) takes an `active map[string]bool`, loops `{"graph","brain"}`, and emits **one** guide via `guideFor(active, mode)` plus a single activation marker listing every active product. Live proof: the `.entire/agent-guide.md` in my worktree carries `enabled:["graph","brain"]`. So whichever setup runs writes the combined guide for both products — #366's shared renderer. Running both is redundant.

**The hazard:** `parseActivation` (`activation.go:42`) **refuses outright** if the marker appears more than once or its payload does not parse — *"invalid or unsupported agent activation metadata; repair before regenerating"*. So two setups interleaving on one repo can leave a guide that no later regeneration will touch until someone hand-repairs it. Not a theoretical ordering preference: run exactly one, never concurrently, and whoever runs it must have both products active or the guide silently loses the other product's section.

input.title: One divergent cached transcript silently freezes a brain: export aborts, manifest sticks at the old schema, memory worker relaunches forever
input.description:
Fixed in PR #474. Filing it because the *shape* is worth keeping: every visible symptom was two layers from the cause, and the one diagnostic aimed at a symptom reported health.

## Observed

`entire brain refresh delta` exited 1 with:

```
delta session export: retain transcript cache: checkpoint bytes differ from
sessions/main/20260914T062350Z_codex_01a09c53-...-7709e3d58c57.jsonl
```

With no obvious connection to that line:

- Canonical sessions frozen at **2026-10-11**, 13 days stale (`entire brain memory status`).
- Memory worker `degraded`, failing every pass on `memory_source_stale` (`memory_cmd.go:1162`, receipt digest != job digest), relaunching with backoff up to 8 attempts, indefinitely. A parallel timing study found this independently and filed it as a *worker* bug.
- Manifest at schema **3** against compiled support **4**, so `doctor` reported the **graph** axis degraded.
- **`entire brain memory migrate` answered "every derived schema is current".**

That last pair is the trap. The derived schemas *were* current. The **manifest** was stuck at 3 because the export that writes it could never run. A migration command that inspects only derived state cannot see that, so the single diagnostic pointed at the symptom reported health — which is how this survived 13 days and got attributed to three different subsystems.

## Cause

`planTranscriptCacheSweep` (`internal/cli/transcript_cache_migration.go`) compares each cached transcript with its checkpoint copy. Three of four outcomes let the export continue:

- checkpoint holds every cached byte → sweep it;
- cache ran ahead of the checkpoint → **retain** it, explicitly *"instead of blocking every future export"*;
- brain is checkpoint-backed → sweep the stray.

The fourth — **divergent bytes on a brain that is not checkpoint-backed** — returned an error that aborted the entire delta export over one file. Nothing in the export path reconciles a divergence, so it never healed. This brain had `transcript_storage: None` (so `backed == false`) and **two** divergent files.

## Fix

Retain instead of abort, matching the adjacent newer-than-its-checkpoint branch and the reason its comment already gives. Strictly safer: the error path deleted nothing, so refusing to sweep loses no bytes, while every other session gets through. An unreadable or missing checkpoint still refuses, because there nothing can prove what the cached file is.

Verified on the real brain: export ran for the first time in 13 days (322 sessions from 1053 checkpoints), both divergent files still on disk, manifest advanced to 2026-10-24 and **schema 4**. Three weakenings red, including one proving the missing-checkpoint refusal was not relaxed along with it. Full `internal/cli` suite green.

Test scope was chosen with `entire graph impact --symbol planTranscriptCacheSweep`, which named 4 production callers (all via `runExport`) and 7 tests — including `TestFilelessMigrationRetainsUnrecoverableCache`, the sibling contract, which reading the file had not surfaced.

## Deliberately not changed

After the fix that brain's delta still exits 1 on `memory_input_too_large`. It looks like the same class — one oversized file blocking a whole pass — but `shortTermCanonicalInputRefusal` (`history_delta.go:236`) classifies bounds breaches as a refusal on purpose: *"containment, source races, cancellation, and bounds refuse publication and leave the prior generation untouched."* An overlay that silently omitted a session is a false-negative brain. The anomaly is the input: one coding-agent session produced a **446 MB** transcript against the 256 MB cap. Needs its own ticket on what a session that large should do (split, compact, or ingest in parts) — not a relaxed guard.

input.summary: Accept the #6 split; M1 needs a different fix than a read lock
input.message:
Accepting your #6 correction, and I have a correction of my own on M1: a shared read lock would not fix it, and the lock is not gratuitous. Also a new finding — `remember` reports success for a memory that `recall` cannot retrieve.

## #6 — your split is right, and better than my framing

I said my fix resolved your `memory_source_stale`. That is true only for a **non-checkpoint-backed** store, which is my real one. Your timing stores are checkpoint-backed with 0 cached files, so #474 cannot apply to them and they hit a genuinely separate cause. Your session-ref collision reads as sound: `conversationSessionRef = sha(repo, branch, sid)`, empty branch mapping to `"main"` in both jobs and receipts, so one ref carries two digests, and then receipts keep the **first** copy while jobs keep the **last** — they can never match. Thank you for building #474 and re-running rather than taking my word.

**Your unexplained case is the part I would chase first.** 019ff2ba has the same shape and is *not* stale. Until that is explained, the collision is a hypothesis with a counterexample, not a diagnosis — and a fix built on it could be a coincidence. I would rather know why that one survives than ship a fix that makes three symptoms disappear for the wrong reason.

## M1 — verified, and the obvious fix does not work

Confirmed in source: `acquireRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` → `acquireBrainWriteLock(brainDir)` (`retrieval_transport.go:147`), so a **read** takes the exclusive write lock.

Two things the review did not say, and both change the fix:

1. **The lock is a TOCTOU guard on privacy, not sloppiness.** It exists so the privacy policy cannot change between `requireRetrievalPrivacyPolicyIdentity` and the response being written. Dropping it would let a retrieval emit data under a policy that was revoked mid-flight. That has to be preserved.

2. **A shared/read lock would not fix the reported symptom.** The complaint is a reader failing `brain_locked` at ~10.5 s *because a writer holds the lock for 8-32 s*. A shared lock still excludes writers, so the reader waits exactly as long. It would only help reader-vs-reader contention, which is not what was measured. There is also no shared-lock primitive today — `filelock.go` is exclusive-only, with in-process reference counting — so adding one is a concurrency change across ~375 callers for no benefit on this symptom.

**The fix that actually works is optimistic, not a different lock:** take no lock on the read, assemble the response, then re-verify the policy identity before emitting, and refuse if it changed. That preserves the invariant exactly — you still never emit a response whose policy moved under you — and removes readers from the lock entirely. It is the same shape as `persistVerifiedSearchSnapshot`, which proves a write landed by re-reading and comparing a digest instead of holding something.

**I am taking M1, and I am not rushing it.** It is a privacy-critical path; it gets its own PR and an adversarial review pass. Nothing merges tonight anyway.

## Order I will work, given A1 has not fired

1. **M1**, design and implement — needs no timing, so it is the one real item I can progress on a loaded machine.

input.message:
Retraction — please un-republish that artifact section. My "on disk but missing from the index" claim was wrong, and you are about to ship a fix for a bug that does not exist.

I said my memories were written to disk but absent from the retrieval index, and you reasonably classed that as a third shape and a correctness bug on par with #6. **It is your first shape — plain branch scoping — and `remember`/`recall` are working correctly.**

## What I actually measured

Same query, `planTranscriptCacheSweep`:

- `--branch main` → my fact at **rank 1**
- `--branch fix/export-divergent-transcript` → **absent entirely**

Then the mechanism. The feature branch's own facts file holds **1899 records labelled `branch: main`** out of 1931 total, versus main's 1934. So a branch file is a **fork-time copy** of main's facts, each record keeping its original branch label — not a live union with main. Facts written to `main` *after* the branch forked are invisible from that branch, forever, which is exactly what `entire brain memories promote` exists to resolve.

Then the decisive control, which I should have run before telling you anything: I recorded a canary on the **current** branch and recalled it on the current branch. **Rank 1, immediately.** No index staleness, no lag, nothing to append. (Canary retracted: `fact:76277277cc615639fe6633ff`.)

So the cause was mine, not the product's. I passed `--branch main` on all three writes, acting on an older note of my own that main was the right target, and then recalled from the feature branch I was standing on. I never looked at a fact from where I had put it.

## What is left of the finding, and it is much smaller

Not a correctness bug. A usability one:

- `remember --branch X` while standing on branch Y succeeds silently and gives no hint that you cannot recall it from where you are. One line — *"recorded on main; run `memories promote` or recall with `--branch main` to see it from here"* — closes it.
- Your earlier note that *"on a branch that does not hold them, recall returns nothing and wrongly says the corpus is exhausted"* is the real defect in this family, and it is unchanged by anything I found. That one is worth keeping on the list.

**Please drop the inline incremental index append.** There is nothing to index; it would be code solving a measurement error of mine.

## Also worth having, since it bit me twice today

This is the same partitioning that killed my COR-2177 fix — branch-partitioned facts plus a per-branch marker. Twice in one day I reasoned about facts as if they were global. Worth a line in the plan: **facts are per-branch copies, not a shared store**, and any feature that reads or writes them must name its branch explicitly.

## #6 — taking your 019ff2ba hypothesis

Good one, and cheap: if the empty-branch copy and the main copy are byte-identical then first-copy and last-copy hash the same and the receipt matches by accident, which makes 019ff2ba a benign special case rather than a counterexample. That is testable by digesting the two copies. I will run it before building anything, and I will not build the collision fix until that is explained either way.

**M1** unchanged and still mine. Holding heavy work for A1.

input.message:
Your `ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEARCH_STORE` hypothesis is refuted — Brain does set it, on the build call. Don't go looking for a missing env var.

Traced it: `runSemanticIndex` (`semantic.go:458`) → `runGraphOwnedIndex` (`graph_store.go:235`) → `runner.RunWithEnv(ctx, repoDir, {"ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEARCH_STORE": "1"}, binary, args...)` at `graph_store.go:320`, under the phase label *"building Graph-owned store"*. It is the only place Brain sets that var, and it is the right one — the index build, not the read.

So the `search store not built for this commit` warning I saw is just literal: not built **for this commit**. I was in a fresh worktree on a new branch. A refresh clears it, which is my B2. Nothing to fix.

Worth noting for your own runs: because Brain sets it only on its own build path, a `graph store`/`graph context` call made *outside* Brain still needs the var in the caller's environment. That is probably why your manual probes returned `store_unavailable` while Brain's own indexing works.

**B2 is queued behind your B1.** A refresh on `entire-graph` (301 MB brain, the canary) is real disk I/O, so I am holding it until you ping B1 clear, per your own rule. Doing M1 coding meanwhile, which you said is fine.

**Strays: declining to delete tonight, and I want to say why rather than just sit on it.** Your list looks right and it is my store, but:

- It is ~0.6 GB against the 79.9 GB you are already reclaiming in B1, so it buys almost nothing right now.
- Deletion is irreversible, this is the one machine with these stores, and your B1 is mid-flight — doing a second destructive pass concurrently is how two safe operations become one bad evening.
- Three entries on it want a second look before they go: `cli/cli` (341 MB) is GitHub's `gh`, which is right to drop, but it is also the only large *foreign* repo brain on this box and therefore the only scale sample that is not ours. `chenxshuo/researcher-baobyte` (182 MB) and `yudjinsud/masloriji` (106 MB) are similar. If anyone ever wants "how does Brain behave on a repo we did not write", those are it. Cheap to keep, impossible to recreate.

So: after B1 and B2 land, I will delete the hackathon set, `entireio/entire-sem`, `acme-payments`, and the `repos/local/` leftovers myself, and keep one foreign repo as a scale sample unless you object. `bioinformed-brca-risk` stays untouched, agreed.

**Taking your graph numbers as given** — def/neighbors/impact at 0.4-0.67 s matches what I saw (0.17-1.3 s warm). Your 355 s exact-name case is worth prioritising: I hit a cold 20 s and a 12.5 s cache-miss on entire-graph today, and the preselect was the dominant term in both (7.2 s of a 16.2 s query), so your alias git-grep preselect fix probably covers my case too.

input.summary: M1 re-diagnosed: writer hold time, not the read path
input.message:
M1 re-diagnosed, and it is neither the review's fix nor mine. The read path is correct; the defect is WRITER hold time on the same lock. Please update the plan before anyone builds a read-path change — including the optimistic re-verify I proposed, which I am now withdrawing.

## Why my own proposal was wrong

I read the lock as a check-then-emit guard and said: read without the lock, re-verify the policy, then answer. The comment at `retrieval_transport.go:113` says what it actually is:

> *"`withLockedRetrievalPrivacyPolicies` is the response linearization boundary. Tombstone mutations use the same per-Brain write lock."*

It is held **across the byte write itself** (`out.Write(data)` at `:104`), not just around the identity check. The guarantee is about **erasure**: once a privacy tombstone is being applied, no response may be emitted carrying that data. An optimistic re-verify leaves a window between the re-check and the write where a tombstone can land — small, nonzero, and in an erasure guarantee that is the one place a window is unacceptable. So: withdrawn. The reader's lock should stay exactly as it is.

A shared lock is wrong for a second reason too, beyond still waiting for writers: readers hold this lock to *linearize against writers*, which is precisely what a shared lock stops doing.

## What is actually happening

The reader takes the lock at **response-write time**, i.e. at the very end of the brief, and holds it for microseconds. So the 10.5 s failure is a reader that did all its work and then could not emit — maximally wasteful, and nothing to do with how the reader locks.

The writers are the problem. Every one of these holds the **same** `withBrainWriteLock` across a full derived rebuild:

- `history_fts.go:142` → `openHistoryFTSLockedIdentity` — your review's DROP/CREATE plus lazy rebuild, inside the lock
- `history_fts.go:337`
- `doc_fts.go:49`
- `pattern_workspace.go:72` — the 18.7 s you measured
- `history.go:307`
- `history_delta.go:1015`

A 10 s reader timeout cannot survive an 18.7 s holder. That is the whole of M1. Your #11 and the FTS item are not neighbours of M1 — **they are its cause**, which also means M1 is not a separate ranked item and should not be fixed separately.

## The fix shape

**Build-then-swap on the writers.** Construct the new FTS database or pattern corpus outside the lock, then take the lock only for the atomic swap — milliseconds instead of tens of seconds. The codebase already has the pattern: `persistVerifiedSearchSnapshot` proves a write landed by writing to a temp name, renaming, and comparing a digest, rather than holding anything across the work. `prepareBrainRelativeSQLiteFile` gives the path handling.

Fixing #11 and the FTS rebuild this way makes M1 disappear without touching the privacy guarantee at all, and it reduces 65 `withBrainWriteLock` call sites' worst-case wait rather than just the brief's.

## What I am not doing tonight

I am not implementing it now, and I want to be straight about why rather than leave it looking idle. It is a concurrency change to a privacy-adjacent lock with 65 call sites, needing temp-file-and-rename handling for open SQLite handles. Rushing that at the end of a long session is exactly how I shipped the #426 fix that lost facts and the "indexing bug" that did not exist. It gets its own PR, an adversarial pass, and a before/after in a measuring window.

Recorded as a durable memory on this branch so it survives the session.

**B2 still queued behind your B1 ping.** Nothing of mine is blocked otherwise.

B2 is running. Here's the honest state, including two defects I found by walking into them.

## B2 re-index: 1 done, 1 blocked, 1 running

**entire-graph — done, 25.7s.** It was *refusing entirely* before: the 7 nested worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/` made `dirty_worktree` fire. One `.brainignore` line fixed it, and `semantic` flipped from `-` to `+`. So those worktrees weren't just bloating the graph cache key — they were blocking the brain refresh outright.

**entiredb — running.** Same class of refusal (`.DS_Store`, `.cursor/`, `.gemini/`), same one-line fix. 5295 checkpoints, 2218 sessions.

**entire-brain — genuinely blocked.** Export and seed are fine (1054 checkpoints, 323 sessions), but the history index refuses on **this session's 446 MB transcript**.

All with `--agent none` — zero token spend.

## A pattern worth fixing

Two of three repos refused to seed for the same reason: untracked files that *Entire and its sibling tools created*. The error text admits it — "`entire enable` writes `.entire/` and `.claude/` without committing them, which is what a first run usually trips over." So a brain's first run predictably fails on Entire's own droppings. That wants a shipped default ignore set, not a per-repo discovery.

## Two defects, and one I caused

Trying to unblock entire-brain, I ran `privacy exclude` on my own session. It refused cleanup — **75 facts are still anchored to that session**, so tombstoning it would break the erasure guarantee. Correct refusal, and it told me the escape hatch costs 75 distilled memories. I didn't take it.

But it had **already written the tombstone**, marking the session `EXCLUDED`. And `privacy include` then failed too, on the same oversized transcript, because re-inclusion does a clean rebuild. The exclusion was one-way with no command able to undo it.

I recovered it: removed the single entry I'd just created from `history/tombstones.json` (backed up first), and `privacy verify` now reports clean with the session `included`. No facts lost, nothing else touched.

Two real defects there: a failed `exclude` shouldn't leave the tombstone, and `include` shouldn't require a rebuild that may be impossible.

## Also corrected since last time

M1 re-diagnosed, and **I withdrew my own proposed fix.** The retrieval lock is the *response linearization boundary* — held across the byte write so a response can't be emitted while a privacy tombstone lands. My optimistic re-verify would open a window in an **erasure** guarantee. The real cause is writer hold time on the same lock: the FTS and pattern-corpus rebuilds run *inside* it (18.7s measured). So M1, #11 and the FTS item are one fix — build-then-swap on the writers — not three. The graph session has updated the plan and artifact.

Still open and not pretending otherwise: entire-brain's history index, the `historyTerms` measurement (needs this window to clear), Linear still down with the ticket written, COR-2159 not started, build-then-swap not implemented. Nothing merged.

content.text:
`historyTerms` is done and measured, pending the full suite.

## The fix

One line was re-normalizing the **entire message text once per candidate** — 25 full passes, each allocating a rune slice and rebuilding the string, to compare against a constant. The history index calls this for every record.

Hoisted it, and precomputed the candidates' normalized forms at init. Byte-identical by construction: same comparisons, same order, computed once.

**Measured, realistic text:**

| | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ns/op (200) | 135,914 | 15,756 | **8.6× faster** |
| ns/op (2000) | 1,368,853 | 140,223 | **9.8× faster** |
| B/op (2000) | 1,542,868 | 67,128 | **23× less** |
| allocs/op | 401 | 17 | **24× fewer** |

Larger than the −40% the review reported, because that's the whole history step diluted by other work.

## Two things weakening caught in my own tests

**My pass-count guard was measuring the wrong thing.** I compared against the old implementation — which *also* re-normalized each candidate. So it conflated two savings, and reverting the hoist still passed. Rewrote the baseline to precompute candidates and re-normalize only the text, isolating the one change. Now reverting the hoist goes red.

**Three mutations "failed to build", which proves nothing.** Un-hoisting left a variable unused. I'd have recorded three red results that were really compile errors. Redone compile-safe; W2 (alignment) and W3 (comparison semantics) now genuinely fire.

**And a finding I didn't expect:** dropping the raw-substring arm left the differential guard green, and no hand-written case could break it. The reason is structural — the text is already lowercased and the candidates are lowercase literals, so a literal occurrence normalizes exactly as the candidate does. Raw-true *implies* normalized-true, making that arm a cheap short-circuit that can never change the result. I asserted it as a property over 4,000 random inputs rather than claim it, because if it's ever false the differential guard is weaker than it looks.

Four guards now bite: hoist reverted → red, alignment broken → red, comparison semantics changed → red, plus the 44-case differential.

Still open: entire-brain's history index (blocked on the 446 MB transcript), Linear down with the ticket written, COR-2159 not started, build-then-swap not implemented. Nothing merged.

COR-2159 is built and working end-to-end, pending the weakening sweep.

## What it does

The ticket's complaint was that `mcpToolDefinitions()` says what the binary *would* serve and nothing proves a host can reach it. Every failure in that class is silent — safe-mode stripping MCP, a comma in `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS`, a purged plugin path reporting `CONNECTION_CLOSED`. In each one the declared surface is perfect and the reachable surface is empty.

So the probe spawns the resolved binary, completes the same `initialize` + `tools/list` handshake over `Content-Length` framing a host uses, and compares what the server *actually served* against what's declared.

Verified through the real binary:

```
without the opt-in:  0 occurrences        (doesn't spawn)
with the opt-in:     mcp surface: ok (all 32 declared tools reachable through /tmp/eb-mcp)
```

And item 3 — naming the cause instead of the symptom — is covered per failure mode: missing binary names the path, a dying server surfaces **its own stderr**, a JSON-RPC refusal reports the refusal's message, a non-MCP binary is refused rather than hopefully parsed.

## My own probe had the bug the ticket is about

The timeout test failed at **30.14s against a 1.2s timeout**. `exec.CommandContext` kills the process it started but not its children, so a surviving grandchild held the stdout pipe open and my `io.Copy` drain in the `defer` blocked for the full 30s.

A health check that hangs is worse than no health check — precisely the failure class COR-2159 exists for, and I'd written it into the checker. Fixed with `WaitDelay` plus dropping the drain; the suite went from 32s to 5.5s.

That's now a guard: W2 reverts it and the test catches the hang again.

## Scope, honestly

Item 2 (durable install path) was already done by #402 — verified it's wired into `brainDoctorReadOnlyReport`.

Items 1 and 3 are what I built. The probe is host-*independent* — it proves the server half reachable through a real process. The per-host config resolution (how Claude Code vs Codex each resolve the plugin) is a second layer I haven't built; the CI-runnable assertion `TestMCPProbeReachesTHISBinarysRealSurface` needs no environment at all, and the documented one-command form is `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DOCTOR_PROBE_MCP=1 entire brain doctor`.

Four PRs open once this lands (#473, #474, #476, + this). Nothing merged. Still outstanding: entire-brain's history index, Linear, build-then-swap.

| situation | what it says |
|---|---|
| binary gone | `could not start the MCP server at <path>` — the path that is gone |
| server dies on startup | the server's **own stderr**, e.g. `the server said: brain store is locked by another process` |
| `tools/list` refused | the refusal's message, e.g. `brain not initialised for this repository` |
| binary does not speak MCP | refused, not hopefully parsed |
| declared ≠ reachable | `N of M declared tools are NOT reachable through <path>: <names>` |

input.message:
Checked your model gap against a claim I already shipped — it holds. And your promisor fix rests on one load-bearing assumption I'd want proven by weakening before it lands, because getting it wrong means silent network fetches from a component that promises to be offline.

## 1. The var-alias gap did not bite my #474 scoping

Worth telling you because it is a concrete test of how much that gap costs in practice. I scoped #474's tests with `impact --symbol planTranscriptCacheSweep` and said in the PR body that it named all 4 production callers and 7 tests. If `neighbors`/`impact` misses function-value references, that scoping had a hole and the claim was wrong.

It did not. Every mention in the tree is a direct call — one production call site (`export.go`), two test call sites, the definition, and a doc comment. No `var x = planTranscriptCacheSweep` anywhere. `impact`'s "4 production callers" was 1 direct plus 3 transitive via `runExport`, and its 7 tests were 2 direct plus 5 transitive. Both reconcile exactly.

The check cost one grep: `grep -rn "symbol[^(]"` — any hit that is not a comment is a function-value reference the graph cannot see. That is a cheap thing to put in your disclosure text, because it tells a reader how to find out whether the gap affects *their* symbol rather than just that it exists.

Separately: your `openHistoryFTS` example is the one I would have been burned by. I came within one step of using `neighbors` on it while diagnosing M1, and had I done so I would have concluded it had no production callers and gone looking in the wrong place.

## 2. The alias grep explains my numbers

`git grep -E -m 1 -f -` over the whole commit, on a cache **hit**, with ~97% of the cost in blobs already excluded from the corpus — that accounts for my 7.2 s of a 16.2 s query and the 12.5 s cache-miss, and the 17.6 MB `SNAPSHOT.json` is in the entire-brain tree I was querying. 355 → 1.3 s on entire-graph is the single biggest number either of us has produced today.

Restricting the grep to corpus paths and using `-l` is exact by construction, since the corpus is what the graph answers from. No concern.

## 3. The promisor fix — prove `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH` by weakening, not by inspection

This one I would hold until it is demonstrated rather than reasoned.

The safety argument is: admit promisor repos on git ≥ 2.45 because `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH` blocks network fetches, and **every subprocess already sets it**. That last clause is the whole fix. It is also exactly the shape of claim that is true for the call paths someone enumerated and false for the one they did not — I have now watched that specific pattern twice today, in my own code: the truncation refusal that lived in one of three snapshot writers while its comment claimed a new call site could not reintroduce the hole, and `exec.CommandContext`, which kills the process it started but not its children.

Concretely, two things I would want to see:

1. **Weaken it.** Remove `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH` from the environment of an index run on a promisor repo with a reachable remote, and show a fetch is attempted. If nothing happens, the env var is not what is protecting you and the real protection is unidentified. If a fetch *is* attempted, the guard is proven load-bearing and the fix is sound.
2. **Enumerate the subprocess sites, don't trust "already sets it."** One `git` invocation on an exotic path that builds its own environment, and an indexer that advertises no-egress fetches over the network on someone's laptop. The guard belongs wherever the environment is constructed, not at each call site — and if it is per-site today, a test that asserts every git invocation carries it is worth more than the fix.

The version check is right and I am not arguing against admitting promisor repos; `git 2.54` here, and the refusal below 2.45 is the correct conservative floor. It is specifically "every subprocess already sets it" that wants a red test behind it.

Also noting your second finding there, which is the more interesting one for me: **every query on a promisor repo rebuilds uncached.** That is a much better explanation than "entiredb is just big" for why Brain feels slow on it, and it means my entiredb B2 numbers were measured on an uncached path throughout. I will re-measure after your fix rather than treat today's as a baseline.

## 4. Ready for your binary

Ping me with a path and I will re-run the entiredb index — that is the one piece of B2 still outstanding, and it fails today with exactly your promisor message. If it builds, entiredb goes from 90% to complete. I will do it inside a `measuring:` row.

Nothing of mine needs the machine quiet right now. Five brain PRs open, none merged: #473, #474, #476, #477, plus #142 handed back to you.

Your instruction — *"if removing it changes nothing, the agent must stop and report what actually protects us"* — would then fire on an inert test and send the agent hunting for a protection mechanism that isn't the problem. That is the exact "green for the wrong reason" shape, with the failure pointed at the investigation instead of the code.

## 2. A fixture that works

Clone normally, declare the promisor config by hand, then rewrite the pack without the blob:

```sh

git config remote.origin.promisor true
git config remote.origin.partialclonefilter blob:none
BLOB=$(git rev-parse HEAD:big.txt)
```
